source.title: How Do Induction Heads Actually Work in Transformers With Finite Capacity?

record.file_problem: None; the full post text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports its own behavioral measurements and argues that ideal induction is incomplete and that its proposed explanations do not fit the observed behavior well.
record.gate_note: The post measures induction strength by comparing next-token log-odds on induction and shuffled sequences. It reports qualitative outcomes in text; the plotted token-level values are not stated numerically. The two fine-grained hypotheses are argued about, but the experiment does not identify or intervene on individual heads or test their composition.
record.test_reason: The post measures induction behaviour (AB…A→B log-odds against shuffled sequences) in a small attention-only model. It argues that the idealised induction mechanism described in the Mathematical Framework is incomplete under capacity limits. It does not identify heads or test previous-token composition.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes that induction works for almost all tokens but far from ideally: strength varies by token and bleeds to tokens near B. Neither of the two proposed capacity-aware hypotheses explains the behaviour well. The large B-to-1st-neighbour drop suggests B's presence in context matters beyond either hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a behavioral log-odds comparison between induction and shuffled sequences, rather than identifying or intervening on induction-head circuitry.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with token identity and token role; induction strength also extends to nearby tokens in unembedding space.
record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated.
record.problems: The experiment uses one 2-layer attention-only model. The text reports qualitative summaries rather than numerical values for the plotted outcomes. It measures behavior but does not identify or test the proposed head-level mechanisms.
record.rows_left_out: The post says it plots actual log-odds for fixed tokens “Fab” as A and “ien” as B, but the text gives no outcome for those plots, so no row is recorded. The token-level histogram values are also not stated numerically; the explicit qualitative outcomes are recorded in r1 and r2.

untested.parts: Whether induction heads form by composing with a previous-token head. No heads were identified, ablated or analysed; only input-output behaviour was measured.

missing.what: Top and bottom 10 tokens for A and B powers, with standard errors over 4096 samples. Values are not reproduced in the text, but they would quantify the token-level variation.
missing.locator: Appendix: Top and Bottom 10 Tokens for A and B Powers

record.verdict_notes: One small model; results are qualitative in the text (plots not given numerically). The mechanism (previous-token composition) is assumed rather than tested, so verdicts concern only the input-output behaviour part of V1. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The experiment measures induction-like input-output behavior, not whether heads form by composing with a previous-token head.

relationships.condition: Neel Nanda's 2-layer attention-only model, random-token AB…A sequences
relationships.reason: Induction strength is described as quite high for almost all tokens, and B is boosted above random tokens (r1, r2, r3). The behaviour exists broadly.
relationships.display_finding: Induction strength was high for almost all tokens, and the expected continuation received a larger boost than random tokens.
